items.title: Cognitive load theory shapes instructional design
items.claim: John Sweller's cognitive load theory (1988 onwards) distinguishes three types of load. Which design principle follows directly?

options.text: Always make instructions as long as possible

Minimise extraneous load (poor design) and manage intrinsic load (task complexity) so working memory can devote capacity to germane load (schema formation) — worked examples for novices, problem-solving for experts (expertise reversal effect)

items.reveal_title: Working memory is the bottleneck for learning
items.reveal:
Sweller's theory builds on Miller's 7+/-2 and Baddeley's working memory. Educational applications include worked-example effect (better than problem-solving for novices), modality effect (combining visual + auditory exceeds visual alone), redundancy effect (repeating information harms learning).

David Geary distinguishes 'biologically primary' knowledge (language, faces) that we acquire effortlessly from 'biologically secondary' (reading, algebra) that requires designed instruction. The theory has reshaped UK curriculum guidance (EEF 2018, Ofsted 2019).
items.why: Teaching that ignores working memory limits — long instructions, complex diagrams, novice problem-solving — is measurably less effective. CLT puts a constraint into instructional design.

items.title: The Health Belief Model predicts (some) preventive behaviours
items.claim: Rosenstock's 1974 Health Belief Model proposes that preventive behaviour depends on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers. What's its empirical track record?

options.text: It predicts all health behaviours perfectly

Meta-analyses (Carpenter 2010) find modest predictive power: perceived barriers strongest, perceived benefits moderate, susceptibility and severity weaker. The model under-weights social and emotional factors
It only applies to dental hygiene

items.reveal:
Rosenstock developed the HBM from 1950s public health work on TB screening uptake. It has been applied to vaccination, screening, smoking cessation and COVID behaviours.

Competitors and extensions: Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen 1991, adds intention and perceived control); Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska 1979, stages of change). Behavioural economics (EAST framework: easy, attractive, social, timely) is the more recent UK policy framework.
items.why: Behaviour-change theories provide testable frameworks but rarely explain more than a fraction of variance. Combining them with structural interventions usually outperforms either alone.

items.title: Flow requires challenge matching skill
items.claim: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's flow research (1975 onwards) identified conditions for the optimal experience. What characterises flow?

options.text: Challenge matched to skill (slightly stretching), clear goals, immediate feedback, deep concentration, sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, time distortion

items.reveal:
Csikszentmihalyi's Experience Sampling Method (ESM, 1975) gave participants pagers; when paged at random they noted what they were doing and how they felt. The pattern: deep enjoyment occurred when skill and challenge were both high.

Too little challenge → boredom; too much → anxiety. Sports psychology uses flow frameworks for performance preparation. Critics (Engeser 2012) note flow may be more available in certain activity types and that measurement post-hoc is suspect.
items.why: Flow describes a measurable state but doesn't make it easy to engineer. The conditions can be designed for; the experience can't be commanded.
